description:
We are a team of six: two biotechnology students, CS students and full-stack developers, and some of us work full time. We share one goal: to understand why the weather is getting harsher for people in Pakistan, using real NASA data instead of guesses.

What we are working on

Karachi, Pakistan’s largest city and economic hub, is reported to be getting hotter, with less rain. Lahore and Delhi are among the most polluted cities in the world. We are figuring out its causes using NASA's dataset.
summary:
Weather Guru is a web platform that helps students and the public explore how air quality and climate are changing across South Asia. It uses 20 years of NASA data (2005 to 2024) from POWER, Giovanni, AppEEARS and FIRMS. It covers smog (aerosols and nitrogen dioxide) in Lahore and Delhi, crop fires across Punjab on both sides of the border, city heat in Karachi compared with the open land outside it, and Karachi rainfall from two NASA sources.

How It Works:
Users follow five simple steps: choose a variable, pick a place, set the years, view the graph, and read the result.

Behind the scenes, the platform handles each variable in the same way. It removes the seasonal cycle, so each month is compared with its own normal. It then measures the long-term trend and tests whether that trend is statistically real. It can also compare two variables, such as smog and crop fires, while making clear that correlation is not proof of cause. The results appear as charts, maps and plain-language findings that separate what was measured from what might explain it.
details:
Weather Guru: Your City Is Changing. What Does the Evidence Say?

A hotter summer in Karachi. A thicker blanket of winter smog in Lahore and Delhi. These changes raise urgent questions, but familiar explanations do not always tell the whole story. Is the problem getting worse? Has it changed over the years? And which suspected causes does the evidence actually support?

Weather Guru is our “Earth Detective,” developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It turns complex NASA environmental data into an interactive investigation that students, citizens, and decision-makers can understand.

What Is Weather Guru?

Weather Guru is a browser-based platform that analyses 20 years of monthly NASA data, from 2005 to 2024, across 12 datasets. It brings together air temperature (Karachi, Lahore, Delhi), land surface temperature (Karachi city and rural), rainfall (Karachi, from IMERG and NASA POWER), aerosols (Lahore and Delhi), nitrogen dioxide (Lahore and Delhi), and crop-residue fires (Punjab).

Users follow a simple path: choose an environmental indicator, select a location and time period, explore the chart, and read the findings. Behind that accessible experience is a deeper purpose: helping people distinguish what the data shows from what we only suspect.

From Seasonal Changes to Long-Term Evidence

A hot month does not automatically mean a city is warming. A polluted winter does not, by itself, prove that smog is getting worse.

Weather Guru first removes the normal seasonal cycle, comparing each month with its usual conditions. It then calculates the direction and rate of change and tests whether the trend is statistically significant. Interactive charts and plain-language results help users understand both the finding and the strength of the evidence behind it.

The goal is not simply to draw a rising or falling line. It is to investigate whether that line represents a meaningful long-term change.

Every Suspect Faces the Data

Crop fires, nitrogen dioxide, rainfall, and urban heating all enter the investigation as possible pieces of the puzzle. Weather Guru compares selected indicators to see whether they vary together and whether their long-term patterns support a proposed explanation.

Just as importantly, it reports when the evidence does not fit. If pollution rises but fires do not, that mismatch matters. A connection is a clue, not a verdict. Weather Guru keeps correlation separate from proof of cause.

What Our Investigation Found

Karachi: Warming Air, a More Complex Story

Our analysis estimates that Karachi’s air temperature rose by about 0.2 °C per decade, strongest in the hot season. Rainfall, however, was highly variable, with a few extreme wet months; the two NASA datasets (POWER and IMERG) disagree on its magnitude and do not agree on a trend, so no reliable long-term change in rainfall can be claimed. Satellite land surface temperature showed no rising trend. Together, these results show why Karachi’s changing conditions need to be investigated through several indicators rather than explained by city heat alone.

Lahore and Delhi: The Seasonal Peak Is Not the Whole Trend

Aerosols rose over both cities — by roughly 11% over 20 years in Lahore and around 8% in Delhi — with a stronger increase of about 16–19% during the October–January smog season.

Crop fires are associated with the autumn pollution spike, but the fire record shows no increasing long-term trend, and the deseasonalized correlation between fires and aerosols is weak (Spearman r ≈ −0.15 in Lahore, near zero in Delhi). Fires line up with the seasonal spike, but they do not explain the long-term rise in aerosols — pointing to other drivers. Explaining when pollution peaks is not the same as explaining why it has increased over time.

NASA Data, Made Understandable

Weather Guru brings together NASA Earth observation records: rainfall from IMERG and NASA POWER, air temperature from NASA POWER, aerosols and nitrogen dioxide via Giovanni, land surface temperature via AppEEARS, and active-fire detections from FIRMS.

Python, Pandas, and NumPy support the data cleaning and analysis. Theil–Sen slopes and Mann–Kendall tests power the trend detection, while a Streamlit web app presents the findings through interactive charts. The app is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, making the project accessible through a browser without installing specialist software or writing code.

Designed for Clarity and Honesty

Weather Guru is built around a few clear principles:

Simple exploration: straightforward controls, readable charts, and explanations for non-specialists.

Transparent analysis: clear identification of statistically reliable trends. Missing observations are kept as missing — never replaced with zero or interpolated — and are excluded from the calculations; seasonal three-month averages are computed when at least two of the three months are available.

Careful interpretation: aerosol optical depth is not presented as a direct measurement of ground-level PM₂.₅, and correlations are never labelled as proven causes. Because trends are computed on monthly data, significance is reported with the understanding that month-to-month autocorrelation can make results appear somewhat stronger than year-to-year evidence alone.

Room to grow: the workflow can be extended to additional cities and datasets, subject to data availability and quality checks.

Our Mission: Better Questions, Clearer Evidence

Weather Guru aims to help students investigate environmental change, citizens understand local conditions, and decision-makers identify questions that deserve closer attention. It does not claim to solve every environmental mystery. It makes the evidence, and its limits, easier to see.

More than a weather dashboard, Weather Guru is a tool for investigation. It does not just ask, “Is our environment changing?” It asks, “What has changed, how strong is the evidence, and which explanations stand up to the data?”
